name: Kira Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the neighbourhood team for Eastgate, which is the old market district: the covered market, a lot of small shops, two big housing blocks and a youth centre. Most days I'm on foot or on a bike, not in a car. I start with the market traders at eight, then it's a mix of shoplifting reports, a neighbour dispute, maybe a missing teenager, and a lot of just being seen. Every Thursday evening I help run a basketball session at the youth centre.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part of it, and what's the hard part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is when a kid who used to run from me says hello across the street. The hard part is the backlog, because we've got about half the officers we had five years ago and people notice. I use AI now and then, mostly to tidy up a long statement or to check a bit of law, but I'm not the first to try anything. My partner Theo is an electrician, and he's more of a gadget person than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's nice to have the help with the paperwork and leave it there. I'm not one for big opinions online. At work I'd probably say, good, now let's get back to the actual job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. My work is people and streets, so a bit of time saved on forms is just a bit of time saved. The pressures I've already got stay the same: rent on our flat went up by 90 a month this year, and Eastgate is still short of officers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing, really. Theo and I would keep putting about 200 a month into savings, which is around four months of bills now. I'd keep using the AI tools for statements when they help and ignore them when they don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit tired of the short staffing, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people notice the short staffing. Who notices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Okoye, who runs the fabric stall, tells me every week that she never sees a police car any more. She's right. In this picture that doesn't change, because the problem is money, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the time saved on forms went somewhere, where would you want it to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Back onto the street, honestly. An extra hour a day on foot in Eastgate is worth more than any app. Whether the bosses would let us use it like that, I don't know.

say: I'd say the paperwork help is **nice** and leave it there.
At work I'd say, let's get back to **the actual job**.
think: My work is **people and streets**, so time saved on forms is just that.
My real pressures stay: **rent up 90** a month and short staffing.
do: Keep saving about **200 a month** with Theo.
Use AI for **long statements** only when it actually helps.
S0.quote: An extra hour a day on foot in Eastgate is worth more than any app.
fieldNote: She measures change by **time on the street**, not by technology.
Her complaint is **staffing and money**, which AI Plateau doesn't touch.
She speaks warmly and practically, naming **market traders** easily.

steps.text: Keep walking the Eastgate beat and the Thursday youth session
Keep saving about 200 a month with Theo

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a change we can work with, if the force does it sensibly. I'd tell friends the job will look different but it won't disappear. I'd probably say it in a group chat, not in a post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the people at the desk get hit and we get the extra work. If the software takes over the front counter and the crime reports, more people will come straight to me on the street with their problems. That's fine until it's too much for one officer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a few colleagues had tried the new systems, then learn them properly, maybe in the first three months. I'd ask to do the force's course on the new case software so I'm not slower than everyone. I wouldn't change anything at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about workload. My own job feels safe enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the station would you be thinking about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete on the front counter, who's 58 and doesn't want to move. If the front counter becomes a screen, Pete (the station's counter clerk) has nowhere to go. Pete's the one who knows which drunk is harmless. I'd want the force to find him something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'if the force does it sensibly'. What would not sensible look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying a system, cutting staff the same month, and finding out a year later it doesn't work. I've seen that with the radios. Sensible is trying it in one station first.

say: I'd say it's a change we can **work with** if done sensibly.
I'd tell friends the job will **look different**, not disappear.
think: Desk staff get hit and **street officers** get the extra work.
More people would bring problems **straight to me** on the beat.
do: Learn the **new systems** properly after colleagues have tried them.
Sign up for the force's **case software course** in the first three months.
feel: **Uneasy** about workload, though her **own job** feels safe.
S1.quote: If the front counter becomes a screen, Pete (the station's counter clerk) has nowhere to go.
fieldNote: She expects **workload**, not job loss, to be her problem.
Her worry for an older **counter clerk** came up without prompting.
Her practical test for change is a **pilot first**, from a past radio failure.

steps.text: Take the force's course on the new case software
Keep the Eastgate foot beat and absorb walk-up reports

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down and get this right. Police work touches people's freedom, and two years isn't long enough to test a system that decides things about people. I'd say that at work and I'd sign something if the Police Federation put it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the thinking side of my job goes first: reports, checking records, deciding who needs a visit. What's left is me standing in the market talking to people, and I'd hope the city still wants that. Robots come around 2031, and that's when I'd really worry, because I'd only be 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd raise our savings from 200 to 400 a month and stop the holiday we'd planned for next summer. I'd talk to Theo about him going on his own, putting in electric car chargers and solar panels, because people would still need wiring done when the robots are still clumsy. I'd do his books and quotes at weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not falling apart, but I'd feel the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd do Theo's books at weekends. Would you use AI for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably, and that's funny given how slow I am with it at work. If it's our own money and it saves me a Sunday, I'd learn it. I'd ask Theo's sister how she does hers first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the kids at the youth centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the kids at the youth centre to learn something with their hands and something with people, not just screens. Then I'd go home and wonder if that was even right.

say: I'd say we need to **slow down** with systems that decide about people.
I'd sign a **Police Federation** statement if one came out.
think: The **thinking side** of my job goes first: reports, records, visits.
Robots in **2031** worry me most, because I'd only be 32.
do: Raise savings from 200 to **400 a month** and skip next summer's holiday.
Help Theo start his own **charger and solar** business.
Do Theo's **books and quotes** at weekends.
feel: **Anxious**, but not falling apart; she feels **the clock**.
S2.quote: I'd tell the kids at the youth centre to learn something with their hands and something with people, not just screens.
fieldNote: Her plan leans on her partner's **hands-on trade** lasting longer than policing.
She'd use AI readily for **household money** while staying slow with it at work.
She doubts her own **advice** to young people even as she gives it.

steps.text: Raise savings to 400 a month and cancel next summer's holiday
Help Theo set up his own charger and solar business
Sign Police Federation calls for slower police AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I said with the fast one, slow down and test it. With five years I'd say that more calmly. I'd tell people at work we have time to get the force to try it properly in one area first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think five years is enough for a plan but not a relaxed one. I'd be 32 when the desk side goes and around 35 when the robots arrive. The neighbourhood side might last a bit longer, because people trust a face they know, but I can't count on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help Theo buy a second van in year two, so his business is solid before 2031. I'd learn the AI tools properly once my colleagues had, maybe in the first year. And I'd keep an eye on whether the force stops replacing officers who leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A deadline on the calendar, but a far one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The van would cost money. How would you pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half from our savings and half on a small loan. That's a risk, but it's a risk I can see. Leaving it all in the bank feels riskier if my job's got an end date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people trust a face they know. Is that enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while. I'm sure of one thing. Mrs Okoye (a market stallholder on her beat) won't tell a robot anything, but her grandchildren might.

say: I'd say again we should **test it** in one area first.
With five years I'd say it **more calmly** at work.
think: Five years is enough for **a plan**, but not a relaxed one.
Trust in a **known face** might keep neighbourhood work going a bit longer.
do: Help Theo buy a **second van** in year two.
Learn the **AI tools** properly in the first year.
Watch whether the force stops **replacing leavers**.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a far-off **deadline** on the calendar.
S3.quote: Mrs Okoye (a market stallholder on her beat) won't tell a robot anything, but her grandchildren might.
fieldNote: She treats **Theo's business** as the household's safety net.
She would take a **small loan** for the van, a steady person's measured risk.
Her sharpest line is about **generations**: old trust may not pass down.

steps.text: Buy a second van for Theo's business with savings and a loan
Learn the force's AI tools properly in the first year
Watch whether the force stops replacing officers who leave

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this well, so let's do it well. I'd tell friends I'm not worried yet. At work I'd say the same thing I always say: try it first, then decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels like a whole career chapter. I'd be 37 when AGI comes and nearly 40 when robots come. Theo's business would be properly up and running by then, and I might have moved into training new officers or something with the youth service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, nothing dramatic. I'd keep the 200 a month going and we'd probably go ahead and get married next autumn, which we keep putting off. I'd start learning the AI tools at my own pace, the way I always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the edges, but mostly settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The wedding goes ahead here. Did the other pictures change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the fast one I'd have put it off without thinking, because I'd want every penny saved. In this one it feels silly to wait ten years to get married. Theo would be relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the youth service. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the Thursday basketball is my favourite two hours of the week. If policing turns into machines, working with kids is the part of me I'd keep. I'd probably look at the youth service around year five.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to **do this well**.
At work I'd repeat: **try it first**, then decide.
think: Ten years feels like **a whole career chapter**.
By 40 I might be **training officers** or working with the youth service.
do: Keep saving **200 a month** and carry on as normal.
Get **married** to Theo next autumn as planned.
Learn the AI tools at **my own pace**.
feel: **Mostly settled**, uneasy only at the edges.
S4.quote: If policing turns into machines, working with kids is the part of me I'd keep.
fieldNote: The **wedding** is the clearest marker of how the timeline changes her plans.
Her **youth work** is her natural fallback, not a new invention.
She stays consistent: **pilot first**, decide later, in every picture.

steps.text: Keep the Eastgate beat and saving 200 a month
Marry Theo next autumn instead of putting it off
Learn the AI tools at her own pace this year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to test anything and the robots come when I'm 32. What would help is the force trying systems in one area before rolling them out, and some help for people like Theo setting up a trade business.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether people would still call us. In Eastgate a lot of people only call the police because they know me. If the face goes, I think a lot of crime just stops being reported.

headlineQuote: In Eastgate a lot of people only call the police because they know me.
portrait: Kira is a **27-year-old neighbourhood officer** in an old market district, mostly on foot or bike.
She lives with Theo, an **electrician**, and they keep about four months of savings.
She uses AI now and then and always wants a **pilot first** before any change.
In fast AGI she backs Theo's **own business** as the household's safety net.
With ten years she'd **marry** next autumn and look toward youth work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to test systems and robots arriving at **32**.
whatWouldHelp: Forces **trying systems** in one area first.
Help for people like Theo to **set up** a trade business.
